conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that high-quality, longer-term evidence shows saw palmetto does not meaningfully improve BPH symptoms compared to placebo, clearly rejecting the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
Based on the evidence, the answer is actually **no**—the best-quality, large-scale, longer-term trials do not show saw palmetto to be superior to placebo for BPH symptoms.

The updated Cochrane systematic review (2012) concluded that "Serenoa repens is no more effective than placebo in relieving urinary symptoms associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia, but it appears to be relatively safe" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20941857/). This built on the largest placebo-controlled trial to date, the STEP study, and other pooled RCT data.

The one-year randomized STEP trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine similarly found "saw palmetto was not superior to placebo for improving urinary symptoms and objective measures of benign prostatic hyperplasia" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085).

The subsequent CAMUS trial extended this further, testing standard and triple doses over 18 months in 369 men. This rigorous, longer-term, dose-escalation study also found no benefit over placebo on lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to BPH (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3326341/).

Earlier, smaller trials and meta-analyses (including an original 2002 Cochrane review) had suggested mild-to-moderate improvements with saw palmetto, and some small industry-linked or short-duration studies (e.g., using specific oil formulations) continue to report positive results. However, the larger, longer, and more rigorously designed placebo-controlled trials—STEP and CAMUS—along with the updated Cochrane meta-analysis, consistently show no significant benefit over placebo.

**Conclusion:** The weight of high-quality, longer-term evidence indicates saw palmetto does NOT meaningfully improve BPH symptoms compared to placebo, contradicting earlier optimistic findings from smaller studies.
